**Before the visit**
- Add your appointment date in the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how prepared the notes are and what you could add to make them fuller.
- Pick the most important topics and questions. Three or four is enough.
- Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your list of medications you are taking is up to date.

**During the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is made so it can be read within 1 minute: counts, averages, a heatmap calendar, and questions.
- Start with the question most important to you.
- If your provider uses another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the visit notes are, and what they are not**

They are a summary of what you entered yourself and information you chose to import from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and the patterns in the notes are only a check of whether something is coincidence, not evidence of a cause. Your provider may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is natural.

**After the visit**

If you started a new medication, add it with its start date. After a few weeks MenoMap can show your records from before and after, which makes the next check-in easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a point in time. It is the day when 12 consecutive months have passed with no period that is not explained by other reasons such as pregnancy, some medications, or surgery. On average in many countries it comes in the early 50s, but anywhere between the mid-40s and mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier or lighter, or closer together or further apart. Changes commonly associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes, and mood changes, often start during this stage when periods are still present. Perimenopause can be a few years or considerably longer, and looks different for each person.

**Postmenopause** is all the time after that 12-month point. Some symptoms settle over time, and some can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of surgery removing the ovaries, some cancer treatments, or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is also called premature ovarian insufficiency, and is worth discussing with your provider.

**How do you know.** For many people over 45, providers judge perimenopause or menopause from medical history and symptoms. Hormone levels vary greatly from day to day, so a blood test is not always necessary. It is used more when you are younger or the situation is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in now. Instead it honestly records what you notice, that is hot flashes, sleep, mood, and treatment, so that you and your provider can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Providers call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden rush of heat, mostly appearing on the face, neck, and chest, sometimes with the face turning red, sweating, a racing heart, or chills afterward. A night sweat is the same thing happening during sleep, and can be severe enough to wake you or soak the bedding.

It is one of the most common changes around menopause. Some people get it a few times mildly, and some get it many times a day so that work and sleep are disrupted. Some people it goes away within a few years, and some it continues much longer.

**Things that can make it easier to happen.** Many people notice patterns related to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress, and thick bedding. These factors vary greatly between people, so recording your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There can be other causes.** Flushing and sweating can be due to thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety, or other conditions. If the symptoms do not match the common pattern or come with weight loss, fever, or feeling unwell, tell your provider.

**To explain it well.** Information helpful at a visit:
- Roughly how many times in the day and at night
- How strong it feels and how long it lasts
- What it interferes with: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What you think came before it
- What you have tried, and whether anything changed

MenoMap's hot flash button and log-later feature exist exactly to keep this information without much effort.

**You can get help.** There are hormone treatments and non-hormone treatments, and things you can try in real life. Which suits you is something to discuss with your provider.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone replacement therapy (commonly called HRT or MHT) supplements some of the estrogen the body makes less of around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can help with other symptoms too.

**There are several forms:** patches, gels, sprays, pills, and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. People who have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks differ by person:** they depend on age, how long since periods stopped, your own and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, heart disease), and the type of treatment and route of administration. So it is not something an app can decide, it is a decision to make together with a provider who knows your history.

**Common questions:**
- Could hormone replacement therapy be an option for me? Why?
- What kind and form do you recommend? Why?
- What benefits can I expect, and how soon will they appear?
- What is my personal risk, and how does it compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should we check again?

**If you are already using it,** record it in MenoMap (Me → Medications). MenoMap shows hot flashes before and after starting. This is a coincidence check, not evidence, and it becomes concrete material to discuss at a check-up.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping, or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone replacement therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply prefer other methods. There are several methods.

**Prescription treatment.** There is evidence that some non-hormone medications reduce hot flashes. This includes some medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class of medication made specifically for hot flashes. Each has different benefits, side effects, and interactions, so a provider can help weigh them.

**Counselling and mind-body therapy.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) tailored to menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats feel less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Real-life changes that help many people:**
- Layers that come off quickly
- A fan at the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and reducing your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help)
- Regular activity and consistent sleep habits

**Supplements and herbal products.** For many, the evidence is mixed or lacking, quality is inconsistent, and some interact with other medications. Tell your provider or pharmacist everything you take, including over-the-counter medicines.

**Change one thing at a time.** MenoMap's 2-week experiment compares your records before the change and during it. It is easier to judge than by feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most visits are short, and it is hard to recall a month of nights on the spot. People tend to recall the most recent or the hardest day. A simple record fills that gap.

**What a symptom diary gives your provider:**
- Not just that the symptom exists, but how often and how strongly it appears
- Whether it is getting better, getting worse, or staying the same
- What was happening around then: sleep, drinking, stress, medications
- A starting point to compare against when trying a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary helps only if you write it consistently. MenoMap is built with a one-tap hot flash button and a four-question evening check-in, so a few seconds is enough without filling a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Records over 2 to 4 weeks usually show a clearer picture than one hard week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most: the most distressing symptom, what you want to try or avoid, anything you are worried about. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you pick questions and print them with the notes.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a healthcare provider**. This is true even if it was only once, or even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most turn out to have a cause that is not serious. For example, thinning of the vagina or the uterine lining is common. But postmenopausal bleeding can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat the earlier it is found. So public health guidance says to get examined rather than wait.

**If you are on hormone replacement therapy,** there may be an expected bleeding pattern depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is not expected from the treatment, heavier bleeding than usual, or bleeding at a time other than expected should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your provider or a medical facility and say you had postmenopausal bleeding.
- Write down the date, the amount, and anything else you noticed. You can keep it in MenoMap (Me → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. It lets you know to get it checked, and includes it in your visit notes for you.

backTranslations.529:
Sleep problems are one of the most common concerns in midlife, and it is rare for there to be a single cause.

**Night sweats** sometimes wake you directly, and sometimes make it hard to fall asleep again because it is too hot or damp.

**Other common factors:**
- Having to get up at night to urinate
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol: it may help you fall asleep but tends to make sleep in the later part of the night broken
- Late caffeine
- Pain, restless legs, or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing: they can be signs of sleep apnoea (especially if you are very sleepy in the day, worth mentioning)

**What helps many people.** A cool, dark room, breathable bedding and easy-to-remove layers, a consistent wake time, and drinking less before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured and well-studied method, and many providers can point you to it.

**What to record.** For 1 to 2 weeks note your sleep score, night hot flashes, alcohol, and late caffeine. It takes just a few taps with MenoMap's evening check-in and hot flash log. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app next to night sweats. As reference information, not an explanation.

**When to get checked.** If sleep problems affect safety (for example driving), mood, or daily life, or if you notice breathing stopping or gasping at night, talk to your provider.
